candidate-models.t: Three models enter the comparison: the **baseline rule**, the **logistic-style** model and the **tree-style** model at depth 4. They differ in complexity, and no winner has been chosen yet.

same-data.t: Each model is **fitted on the same 700 training customers** and **judged on the same 150 validation customers**. Otherwise differences in score might just be differences in data.

same-protocol.t: The checklist: same training data, same validation set, **same metrics**, and the test set kept **out** of the comparison. A fair comparison changes only the model.

metric-table.t: Each row is one model on the validation set. The tree has precision **0.59**, recall **0.80** and F1 **0.68**. The last column asks whether each model meets the stated goal.

performance.t: The recall column is highlighted because it is the goal's key requirement. Recall rises **0.40 → 0.70 → 0.80**, and only the tree reaches the **0.75** that is needed.

complexity.t: The tree is the most complex candidate (**3**). More complexity means more to tune, explain and keep stable, so it has to earn its place with better results.

interpretability.t: All three can still be explained to retention staff, and the tree stays small at **depth 4**. Interpretability does not overturn the metric result here.

select-model.t: The tree row is highlighted: it is the **only model that meets both parts of the goal**. It trades some precision (**0.64 → 0.59**) for more recall (**0.70 → 0.80**).

lock-choice.t: The decision is written down: **tree-style, max_depth 4**. After this point nothing about the model or its settings changes.

test-ready.t: Only now is the **test set** used, **exactly once**, on the locked model. **Remember:** compare fairly, choose against the goal, lock the decision, then run the final test.
